Moth wings have an intricate array of scales that reduce ultrasonic echoes in the 20–160 kHz range.
The acoustic stealth property is an adaptive trait evolved to reduce detection by bat sonar.
The scale layer on moth wings is thinner than the acoustic wavelength (~17 mm at 20 kHz).
Moth scales vary in size and shape, producing a broad range of acoustic resonances.
Butterfly scales, unlike moth scales, increase acoustic reflection in the ultrasonic range.
Experimental measurements and finite-element modeling confirmed the broadband absorption.
The broadband absorption spans from 20 to 160 kHz, matching bat echolocation frequencies.
Moth scales also serve thermoregulatory and optical camouflage functions.
Metamaterials are artificial or natural structures with tailored wave response properties.
Stealth technology in aircraft uses coatings and composites to absorb radar waves.
The concept of acoustic metamaterials has been explored for cloaking devices against microwaves and sound.
Natural photonic crystals in butterfly wings are examples of optical metamaterials.
The study provides evidence that natural selection engineered moth wings as acoustic metamaterials.
The research draws on historical camouflage techniques inspired by natural disruptive patterns.
Acoustic stealth differs from optical stealth by targeting sound wave reflection rather than light.
The moth wing scale array produces an emergent broadband response by coupling acoustic modes.
The study was published online on 18 December 2020 in Nature Materials.
The research team measured acoustic reflections from moth species native to Africa and China.
The moth thorax has a thick layer of hair-like scales that also contribute to acoustic absorption.
The broadband acoustic stealth effect is likely essential for moth survival against diverse bat predators.
